subject: math
cluster: Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers
description: Students add and subtract rational numbers (integers, fractions, and decimals, both positive and negative) by applying and extending previous understandings of addition and subtraction. They interpret sums and differences on horizontal and vertical number line diagrams, understand that $p - q = p + (-q)$, recognize that $p + (-p) = 0$ (additive inverses), and that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, $|p - q|$. They apply these operations to real-world contexts such as temperature change, elevation, and account balances.
subSkills: Add two rational numbers with the same sign (combine magnitudes, keep the sign)
Add two rational numbers with opposite signs (subtract magnitudes, take the sign of the larger magnitude)
Recognize additive inverses: $p + (-p) = 0$ and that $-(-p) = p$
Rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite: $p - q = p + (-q)$
Model addition and subtraction as directed moves on a horizontal or vertical number line
Interpret the distance between two rational numbers as $|p - q|$
Add and subtract rational numbers expressed as fractions (find common denominators) and as decimals
Apply signed addition and subtraction to real-world situations (temperature, elevation, debits and credits)

problemArchetypes.name: Integer sum, same or opposite signs
Fraction addition and subtraction with signs
Number line move interpretation
problemArchetypes.example: Starting at $2$ on a number line, you move $5$ units in the negative direction. Where do you land, and what sum does this model?

problemArchetypes.name: Distance between two rational numbers
problemArchetypes.example: Find the distance between $-3$ and $\frac{5}{2}$ on the number line using $|p - q|$.

problemArchetypes.name: Real-world signed context
problemArchetypes.example: The temperature was $-4^{\circ}\text{C}$ at dawn and rose by $11^{\circ}\text{C}$ by noon. What was the noon temperature?

Easy.description: Single-operation problems with integers or simple fractions/decimals. One addition or one subtraction, no chaining. Number line moves are direct one-step interpretations.
constraints: Operands are integers in $[-20, 20]$, unit-friendly fractions with denominators of $2$, $3$, or $4$, or decimals to the tenths place
Exactly one addition or subtraction step
If subtraction, the rewrite $p - q = p + (-q)$ is the only conceptual hurdle
Contexts are familiar (temperature, money) when present

Medium.description: Requires a sign decision plus a computation step: opposite-sign fraction addition needing a common denominator, signed decimals, or subtracting a negative. Number line and distance problems use non-integer endpoints.
constraints: Fractions require finding a common denominator (e.g., denominators $4$ and $6$) and may need simplification
Decimals extend to hundredths or mix decimals with negatives
Includes subtracting a negative ($p - (-q)$) and additive-inverse solving
Distance problems use one or two non-integer rational endpoints

Hard.description: Multi-step chains of additions and subtractions, mixed number formats (a fraction and a decimal in one problem), or word problems that require modeling the situation as a signed expression before computing. May ask for a comparison or a net result over several changes.
constraints: Three or more operands, or an expression mixing fraction and decimal forms
Requires translating a verbal real-world scenario into a signed sum or difference
May combine a number line interpretation with a distance computation
Mixed numbers must be converted to improper fractions; results may need conversion back to mixed-number or simplified form

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats subtracting a negative as subtracting a positive (drops the double negative)
Student adds the magnitudes when signs are opposite instead of subtracting them
Student keeps the wrong sign on an opposite-sign sum (sign of the smaller magnitude)
Student adds fraction numerators and denominators without finding a common denominator
Student ignores or mishandles the sign when adding signed decimals
Student computes distance as the signed difference rather than the absolute value
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives the distance between $-3$ and $\frac{5}{2}$ as $-\frac{11}{2}$ instead of $\frac{11}{2}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks the additive inverse of $p$ is its reciprocal or leaves the sign unchanged
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says $-\frac{7}{8} + q = 0$ requires $q = -\frac{8}{7}$ or $q = -\frac{7}{8}$ instead of $q = \frac{7}{8}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student moves the wrong direction on the number line for a negative addend
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Starting at $2$ and adding $-5$, moves right to land on $7$ instead of left to land on $-3$
